item.title: [37★] Machine-learning decoders for fusion-based quantum computing in real time
item.author: Daniel Barter, ..., Eddie Richter, Sam Roberts
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 37 ★

Authors: Daniel Barter, ..., Eddie Richter, Sam Roberts

arXiv ID: 2611.13630 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires decoders that combine accuracy, throughput, low latency, and scalability to large numbers of physical qubits. In photonic fusion-based architectures, erasures from photon loss and probabilistic fusion measurements are a dominant error mechanism, motivating decoders that remain accurate at high erasure rates. We introduce PRISM, a transformer-based machine-learning decoder designed to exploit the known locations of erasures in protocols subject to both Pauli and erasure errors. We benchmark PRISM across a wide range of fault-tolerant protocols based on surface codes, color codes, and quantum low-density parity-check codes, with distances up to 24. Across these benchmarks, PRISM matches the logical error rates of integer-programming-based decoders while being significantly faster, including at error rates up to 50% of threshold. We further optimize the decoder and its real-time hardware implementation to reduce latency while maintaining accuracy. Our optimized implementation on an AMD VP1902 FPGA can decode logical blocks of distance 8 in both space and time, demonstrating a latency of 6.59 microseconds and an amortized decoding time of 1.56 microseconds per logical block is possible. These results show that machine-learning decoding can provide accurate, low-latency inference for erasure-dominated fault-tolerant quantum architectures.

item.title: [32★] PriorTilt: Decoding quantum LDPC codes with sparse perturbations of belief propagation priors
item.author: Min Ye, Nicolas Delfosse
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 32 ★

Authors: Min Ye, Nicolas Delfosse

arXiv ID: 2611.13373 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Although belief propagation (BP) is a widely adopted decoder for classical low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes, its accuracy is limited in the quantum setting. We introduce \PriorTilt, a variant of BP obtained by selectively perturbing a small fraction of its prior log-likelihood ratios using offsets determined by recent posterior and outgoing-message statistics, while preserving the same message-passing rules. We compare \PriorTilt with Relay-BP and beam search decoders for circuit-level decoding of three benchmark codes. \PriorTilt achieves a lower logical error rate (LER) than both baselines at every tested data point. For the [[144,12,12]][[144,12,12]][[144,12,12]] Gross code BB144 at noise rate p=10−3p=10−3p=10^{-3}, the LER reductions reach 4.3×4.3×4.3\times relative to Relay-BP and 3.1×3.1×3.1\times relative to the beam search decoder. At p=10−3p=10−3p=10^{-3}, \PriorTilt has lower mean decoding times than Relay-BP on all three codes and achieves mean decoding speedups of approximately 2.6×2.6×2.6\times--3.0×3.0×3.0\times over the beam search decoder. For BB144 at p=10−3p=10−3p=10^{-3}, \PriorTilt achieves an LER approximately 610×610×610\times lower than the standard min-sum BP decoder with the same iteration budget, while perturbing fewer than 0.5%0.5%0.5\% of its priors per round on average.

item.title: [30★] FusionQ: A Generic and Optimal Decoding Framework for Ultra-Low-Latency Quantum Error Correction
item.author: Junyu Zhou, ..., Gushu Li, Yue Wu
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 30 ★

Authors: Junyu Zhou, ..., Gushu Li, Yue Wu

arXiv ID: 2611.13111 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Quantum error correction (QEC) decoding has traditionally been organized around fixed decoding instances: a monolithic space-time detector error model (DEM), or a predetermined temporal window, is handed to a backend decoder after enough syndrome data has arrived. This paper presents FusionQ, a fusion decoding framework that changes this paradigm by deriving local decoding tasks from the observed syndrome and then fusing their results into a single global correction. Instead of forcing every shot through the same global or windowed problem, FusionQ builds open-boundary local DEMs around fired detector clusters and expands the corresponding footprints only when a local optimum uses virtual boundary errors. FusionQ is generic in the decoder backend: the scheduler requires only a local solution and a boundary-use flag, so exact solvers, matching-style decoders on graphlike DEMs, and heuristic decoders can share the same runtime. We prove a compositional optimality theorem: with an exact minimum-weight local backend and boundary-free publication, fusing the published local decoding results yields a global most-likely error (MLE) solution of the original DEM. Our evaluation shows that, with an exact backend, FusionQ matches the monolithic MLE result on every shot. Across decoder backends, FusionQ substantially reduces decoding latency by overlapping local decoding with hardware syndrome acquisition.

item.title: [10★] The energetic cost of loading classical data in quantum computers
item.author: Joao F. Doriguello, Alessandro Luongo, Harshit Verma

Authors: Joao F. Doriguello, Alessandro Luongo, Harshit Verma

arXiv ID: 2611.14422 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Quantum algorithms for machine learning, chemistry, and cryptanalysis often assume coherent access to classical data at negligible physical cost. We instead treat data loading as a hardware process and quantify the dynamic energetic cost of a quantum random access memory (QRAM) query on a superconducting processor. Using the metric-noise-resource framework, we relate query fidelity and power to gate duration, relative two-qubit drive strength, and the distribution of attenuation across a multi-stage refrigerator, while accounting for thermal photons and gate errors. We analyze the linear-depth multiplexer and the noise-resilient bucket-brigade architectures, adapting the latter to a native superconducting gate set and refining its fidelity analysis using the fully decomposed gate schedule. For a representative bucket-brigade QRAM query with a 121212-qubit address register we obtain a query fidelity of 0.9690.9690.969. The query consumes 3.51×10−4J3.51×10−4J3.51\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{J} of dynamic energy, corresponding to an average dynamic power of 4.38W4.38W4.38\,\mathrm{W} and a peak of 64.4W64.4W64.4\,\mathrm{W}. Our optimization shows that, at fixed target fidelity, the operating point and attenuation profile can change the average power by a factor of two or more.

item.title: [10★] A Compiler for Fault Tolerant Quantum Computing
item.author: Narasinga Rao Miniskar, ..., Jeffrey S. Vetter, Travis S. Humble
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 10 ★

Authors: Narasinga Rao Miniskar, ..., Jeffrey S. Vetter, Travis S. Humble

arXiv ID: 2611.13301 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) needs compiler intermediate representations (IRs) that preserve error-correcting-code choices, syndrome information, and non-Clifford resource requirements through analysis, simulation, and hardware lowering. We report practical experience building FTQC, an open-source Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) dialect that makes logical qubits, syndromes, magic states, and Pauli frames typed static single assignment (SSA) values. Its error-correction-aware type system, two-level lowering design, and IR-resident resource analysis provide one inspectable pipeline to Open Quantum Assembly Language~3 (OpenQASM~3), the Quantum Intermediate Representation (QIR), Stim, and IQM hardware. Case studies across three code families show that typed metadata makes code-specific decisions verifiable and retargetable: on the 20-qubit Pathfinder at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, decoding reduced logical readout error by 3.3 times. They also expose hidden architectural costs: for a three-qubit Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT-3), a magic-state factory requires five times the peak qubits of the encoded circuit. These experiences demonstrate a practical foundation for developing and evaluating fault-tolerant compiler transformations across software and hardware targets.

item.title: [9★] Simulating closed- and open-system dynamics of Tavis--Cummings lattices on fault-tolerant quantum computers
item.author: Soumya Sarkar, ..., Nam Nguyen, Gavin Brennen
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 9 ★

Authors: Soumya Sarkar, ..., Nam Nguyen, Gavin Brennen

arXiv ID: 2611.14398 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Tavis--Cummings lattices couple cavities containing several emitters and host polaritonic many-body dynamics whose real-time correlations are costly to compute classically in two dimensions, especially when unequal emitter relaxation or dephasing rates break permutation symmetry. We analyze logical resources for fault-tolerant closed- and open-system simulation of an atom-resolved lattice with LLL cavities, NNN emitters per cavity, and photon cutoff n_maxn_maxn\_{\max}, including target observable estimation. Building on ladder-operator block encoding, we construct circuits for photon hopping and local light--matter exchange and combine them to encode the lattice Hamiltonian. By updating source and destination photon occupations in place, the hopping circuit eliminates the auxiliary L⌈log2(n_max+1)⌉L⌈log2(n_max+1)⌉L\lceil\log_2(n\_{\max}+1)\rceil-qubit photon register used by two-register implementations. Across three uniform-coefficient examples with 161616 to 256256256 cavities, the controlled walk uses 4.754.754.75--8.118.118.11% fewer Toffoli gates than the paired two-register implementation under matched shared preparation, precision, control, and workspace conventions. For closed systems, we implement real-time evolution with generalized quantum signal processing and bound the cost of estimating retarded cavity spectral functions. For open systems with photon loss, emitter relaxation, and dephasing, we use a sampled first-order dilation and bound the runs and timesteps needed to estimate transient photon statistics such as g(2)(0)g(2)(0)g^{(2)}(0). With state-preparation and measurement costs explicit, these estimates provide a reference for assessing fault-tolerant light--matter lattice simulation costs.

item.title: [7★] Syndrome extraction for quantum LDPC codes in silicon: Distributed entanglement and mobile ancillas
item.author: William Chow, Jonathan Baugh
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 7 ★

Authors: William Chow, Jonathan Baugh

arXiv ID: 2611.13371 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes can reduce the number of data qubits required per logical qubit, but their checks require long-range interactions on a planar device. We develop a singlet fabric for bivariate-bicycle codes on a silicon node network. Spin singlets are generated on shuttling lanes and distributed between nodes, where local operations consume them to measure non-local stabilizers. We construct two syndrome-extraction circuits, based on distributed GHZ states and ancilla teleportation, and evaluate them using hardware-constrained schedules and circuit-level memory simulations. We compare these circuits with CAbLECAR, which transports a mobile ancilla between the data qubits of each check. Teleportation can outperform CAbLECAR on its original layout when transport includes spin flips as well as dephasing. Placing the mobile ancilla on our node lattice, however, shortens the mean scheduled route for the [[144,12,12]] Gross code from 350 to 153 μμ\mum and lowers its logical error rate up to 50-fold in the sampled bit-flip regime. Direct transport then achieves a lower logical error rate than either singlet circuit at every sampled Gross-code point. With frequent transport bit flips, the GHZ circuit overtakes direct transport once two-qubit gate and readout errors fall below about 444-5×10−45×10−45\times10^{-4}, roughly half the value assumed here. Fixing the ancilla's data-visit order reveals a trade-off between shorter routes and the correlated errors produced by ancilla faults. Source heralding improves both singlet circuits, whereas phase purification helps the GHZ circuit only above a noise-dependent crossover and worsens teleportation throughout. These results show that the physical layout and interaction order can be as consequential as the choice of extraction circuit, and that cleaner entangled resources do not necessarily produce a more reliable logical memory.

William Chow, Jonathan Baugh

item.title: [6★] Dynamical GKP codes
item.author: Jonathan Pelletier, Baptiste Royer
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 6 ★

Authors: Jonathan Pelletier, Baptiste Royer

arXiv ID: 2611.14081 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Dynamical codes protect quantum information with sequences of measurements, generalizing the stabilizer formalism of static codes. However, the dynamical formalism has been developed exclusively for qubit systems. While Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) codes are promising candidates for quantum computing that encode qubits in the continuous phase space of oscillators, no dynamical formalism has been developed for them. In this work, we bridge this gap and introduce dynamical GKP codes, combining continuous-variable lattice encodings with time-dependent translation measurement dynamics. To obtain the update rules and the distance of a given measurement sequence, we first generalize GKP codes to subsystem GKP codes using scaled symplectic lattices. Building on this structure, we adapt the ancestry, detector, and benign-error machinery originally developed for dynamical qubit codes. From this construction, we obtain a general and efficient method to compute the syndrome and distance of a dynamical GKP code from a persistent stabilizer lattice and a bounded inference window. We illustrate the framework with the example of the two-mode square-hexagonal Floquet GKP code. This code has reduced measurement weight compared to both the square and hexagonal GKP codes, while combining their set of logical gates, resulting in easier implementation of the full single-qubit Clifford group. Finally, we show that measurements with irrational symplectic overlap, which have no analog in discrete qubit codes, reduce to destructive homodyne detection in the single-mode case. These results extend an important qubit-code tool to continuous-variable systems and identify a new bridge between discrete stabilizer measurements and continuous homodyne detection.

Jonathan Pelletier, Baptiste Royer

item.title: [5★] Cross-Platform Benchmarking of GHZ-State Generation in Quantum Processors via Cloud Services
item.author: Sergio Hernández, ..., Rubén Peña, Mikel Sanz
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 5 ★

Authors: Sergio Hernández, ..., Rubén Peña, Mikel Sanz

arXiv ID: 2611.14114 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Quantum computing has rapidly evolved into a diverse ecosystem of hardware platforms that differ in their underlying technologies and operational characteristics. Consequently, benchmarking has become essential for identifying the strengths of quantum processors, comparing their performance, and enabling informed decisions when selecting the most appropriate quantum computing platform for specific applications. In this work, we benchmark nine commercially accessible quantum processors from five vendors, spanning superconducting and trapped-ion technologies, using the multipartite entanglement benchmark from the QuSquare suite. All experiments were performed through remote cloud-access services, with the default compilation of each provider and without error mitigation, reflecting the performance experienced by end users. The benchmark estimates the fidelity of Greenberger--Horne--Zeilinger (GHZ) states by direct fidelity estimation and searches for the largest GHZ state whose fidelity is compatible, within the statistical error, with the genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) threshold F=1/2F=1/2F=1/2. Our results reveal a substantial gap between the total number of physical qubits available on a processor and the size of the largest GHZ state passing the benchmark: the best superconducting processors reach N∗=27N∗=27N^*=27 and N∗=24N∗=24N^*=24 qubits, less than a quarter of their registers, whereas the 12-qubit trapped-ion processor passes with its full register. We further show that median calibration data are poor predictors of the benchmark outcome, and that the reported sizes depend strongly on the statistical decision rule: requiring certified GME reduces the number of devices that succeed at any tested size from nine to four. These results provide a baseline for future cross-platform benchmarking of quantum processors.

item.author: Takumi Yuri, Yu-Xuan Chen, Kenji Toyoda
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 3 ★

Authors: Takumi Yuri, Yu-Xuan Chen, Kenji Toyoda

arXiv ID: 2611.13967 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Vibrational excitations, or phonons, in trapped ions serve as useful resources for quantum information processing, including quantum simulation and computing. Localized excitations of ions' vibrational motion (local phonons) can be used for simulating quantum particles that propagate over a system. Here, we experimentally investigate the propagation of a localized vibrational excitation in a one-dimensional trapped-ion crystal. A 10-ion crystal confined in a harmonic potential is used. It is found that inhomogeneity in the spacing between the ions leads to characteristic behaviors such as adjacent hopping and global movement. A comparison of the experimental results with numerical simulations shows agreement up to fine details. The system explored here may be extended to many-body systems of bosonic particles as well as more complex quasiparticles.

item.title: [3★] How wide must an eavesdropper be? Leakage of a toric-code logical bit to a strip and the Nishimori point
item.author: Konstantinos Karagiannis
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 3 ★

Authors: Konstantinos Karagiannis

arXiv ID: 2611.13174 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Fault-tolerant quantum computers hand pieces of each logical qubit to separate decoder modules and shared readout lines. How much does a piece reveal? We prove that for any region and any Pauli noise, including correlated noise, an observer's optimal advantage in learning a logical bit is exactly 1 - 2 P_fail, where P_fail is the failure probability of maximum-likelihood decoding confined to that region. Two lessons follow. Geometry, not noise, provides the protection: a region that misses a single column of the code learns exactly nothing at any noise level, while a region that spans the code is protected by noise only at impractical distances (d > 350 for one row at a 10^-3 flip rate). And width is a poor guide to risk: under i.i.d. noise a two-row strip learns exactly as little as one row, yet below threshold an eavesdropper needs a width growing only as ln d. Through the identity, the strip's operational threshold is the Nishimori point of the random-bond Ising model, and a Walsh-Hadamard transfer matrix up to width 16 locates it to within a few thousandths. On two IBM Heron processors (d = 3, 5), an emulated strip adversary shows the predicted jump at width three, and non-uniform qubit errors let a trained attacker profit from the second row that uniform noise makes useless. We turn these results into design rules for partitioned decoding and multiplexed readout. Code and data are included.

Konstantinos Karagiannis

item.title: [3★] Frustration-free control for quantum-state preparation: an exact first-passage theory
item.author: T. Dörstel, ..., J. H. Wilson, M. Buchhold
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 3 ★

Authors: T. Dörstel, ..., J. H. Wilson, M. Buchhold

arXiv ID: 2611.13094 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Quantum circuits based on local measurements and feedback can autonomously prepare and stabilize entangled many-body states. In frustration-free control, the target manifold is specified by local constraints, whose violations are detected by measurement and removed by feedback. We develop an exact theory of this mechanism for the preparation of Dicke states of NqNqN_q qubits. Dicke states span the permutation-symmetric subspace, one per magnetization sector. Local singlet projectors define the constraints and detect departures from permutation symmetry. The resulting dynamics closes exactly on the span of the Nq(Nq−1)/2Nq(Nq−1)/2N_q(N_q-1)/2 singlet-pair projectors and is equivalent to a classical first-passage process: measurements move the pair endpoints, while feedback absorbs pairs on measured bonds. The closure reduces the exponentially large many-body Liouvillian to a generator of polynomial size. In one dimension we solve this process in closed form. Its slowest rate, 2[1−cos(π/Nq)]2[1−cos(π/Nq)]2[1-\cos(\pi/N_q)] in units of the measurement rate, is an exact Liouvillian eigenvalue. For any scheme of this class, the relaxation time is bounded below by the inverse fraction of pair configurations on which feedback acts; local feedback reaches O(Nq)O(Nq)O(N_q) of O(N2q)O(N2q)O(N_q^2) configurations, requiring a time at least linear in NqNqN_q. A second exact closure determines the final state reached from any initial condition. Extensions to modified transport, restricted feedback, and physical errors yield an exact transport-to-absorber crossover, geometric preparation laws, and a bound on the stationary leakage. An exact second-moment closure determines the ensemble fluctuations: the measurement noise is conserving, while feedback generates removal shot noise and pair correlations. Preparation, acceleration, robustness, and fluctuations are thus governed by one exactly solvable process: the transport and absorption of local constraint violations.

item.title: [2★] Nonperturbative string dynamics in a (2+1)D lattice gauge theory on a superconducting quantum processor
item.author: Sanziana Stelea, ..., Jad C. Halimeh, Ivano Tavernelli
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 2 ★

Authors: Sanziana Stelea, ..., Jad C. Halimeh, Ivano Tavernelli

arXiv ID: 2611.14484 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Electric flux strings underpin confinement in gauge theories. In two spatial dimensions, their evolution involves competing processes of charge motion, pair creation, and transverse deformation. Accessing these dynamics beyond perturbative limits challenges classical approaches, as entanglement growth restricts the times accessible to tensor-network simulations. Here we use quantum simulation to investigate a (2+1)D Z2 lattice gauge theory with dynamical matter and an explicit magnetic plaquette interaction, spanning strongly confined and nonperturbative deconfined regimes. Using 63 superconducting qubits, including 12 ancillas, we evolve initially localized strings with static or dynamical endpoint charges. Spatially resolved measurements reveal rapid charge and flux spreading in the deconfined regime, enhanced matter occupation in the string interior near the pair-creation resonance, and suppressed spreading at strong electric fields. String-path occupations further probe transverse rearrangements between configurations connected by plaquette operations. Retaining separate matter and gauge degrees of freedom makes local Gauss-law constraints directly accessible for error detection. Combining these constraints with ancilla checks and noise rescaling, we measure dynamics in circuits containing up to 15 second-order Trotter steps. Our results establish quantum simulation as a practical approach to exploring nonperturbative string dynamics in two spatial dimensions, with gauge redundancy serving as an experimental resource.

Sanziana Stelea, ..., Jad C. Halimeh, Ivano Tavernelli

item.title: [2★] Implementing rapid reset of superconducting qubits with on-chip dissipation
item.author: Feiyu Li, ..., He Wang, Fei Yan
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 2 ★

Authors: Feiyu Li, ..., He Wang, Fei Yan

arXiv ID: 2611.14391 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Rapid and high-fidelity qubit reset is essential for quantum state initialization and quantum error correction. Conventional reset protocols for superconducting qubits often rely on dissipative elements connected to external circuitry, exposing qubits to thermal noise from higher-temperature environments. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a scalable approach to qubit reset and leakage removal over multiple transmon qubits using dedicated dissipation units comprising resonators coupled to on-chip resistive loads. This architecture provides Purcell protection while isolating the qubits from warmer external circuitry. We achieve a median reset time constant of approximately 48 ns for the |g⟩−|e⟩|g⟩−|e⟩|g\rangle-|e\rangle transition, with an effective bath temperature of 30 mK. A 400-ns reset pulse yields residual excited-state populations of 0.29%0.29%0.29\% and 0.67%0.67%0.67\% for qubits initialized in |g⟩|g⟩|g\rangle and |e⟩|e⟩|e\rangle, respectively. We further demonstrate efficient leakage removal from the |f⟩|f⟩|f\rangle state, reducing its residual population to 0.51%0.51%0.51\%. These results establish a simple, reproducible, and easy-to-integrate approach to dissipation engineering in superconducting quantum processors.

Abstract:

Many image classification tasks have labels that are unchanged by rotations and reflections. Equivariant quantum neural networks incorporate such symmetries by design, but the specific benefit of symmetry is difficult to isolate. Equivariant quantum circuits are usually compared with architectures that also differ in gates, structure or size. Here, we investigate the role of invariance in a controlled setting, classifying images whose labels are invariant under the dihedral group D4D4D_4. We compare four eight-qubit models with identical encoding, circuit structure and number of trainable parameters, and equivalent dynamical Lie algebras, and benchmark invariant implementations against non-invariant ones in terms of generalization error, robustness to shortcut learning and resilience to a realistic noise model. On four binary tasks, including MNIST and two scientific data sets of galaxies and red blood cells, the invariant models trained on a few tens of images show better generalization than non-invariant ones. Invariance also makes the models immune to orientation shortcuts: when trained with a class-dependent corner watermark, the non-invariant models learn the watermark and often drop to chance level when it is moved. We show that the gain in accuracy of invariant models persists also under a realistic noise model.

Giuseppe D'Ambruoso, ..., Giuseppe Magnifico, Cosmo Lupo

item.title: [2★] A New Computational Model for the Spin-Free Sum-of-Squares Energy Bounds of Electronic Hamiltonian
item.author: Yuming Bao, ..., Dongdong Ge, Yinyu Ye
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 2 ★

Authors: Yuming Bao, ..., Dongdong Ge, Yinyu Ye

arXiv ID: 2611.14319 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Optimizing spin-free sum-of-squares (SOS) energy bounds for electronic Hamiltonians leads to semidefinite programs whose expanded size grows rapidly with the orbital dimension. We derive an exact reformulation of an established spin-free SOS model as a convex quadratic problem over a single symmetric matrix constrained between zero and the identity. Explicit recovery maps connect feasible quadratic-program iterates to certificates in the original SOS formulation, and identify the Frank--Wolfe gap with the separation between recovered primal and dual objectives. We implement the quadratic action through GPU-accelerated Coulomb contractions and solve the reformulated problem using a cached implementation of fully corrective Frank--Wolfe, referred to here as the dimension-reduced simplicial method (DRSM) that caches operator products and optimizes convex-combination weights in a small corrective quadratic program. Numerical experiments cover 65 FCIDUMP models, molecular geometries, and regular hydrogen rings, including original-coordinate recovery checks on nine instances and comparisons with FISTA and a boundary-point SDP solver. On eight H100 GPUs, a cold-start calculation for C720720_{720} with 10,080 spatial orbitals reaches a freshly recomputed Frank--Wolfe gap of 8.82×10−98.82×10−98.82\times10^{-9} hartree in 5.02 hours. Full-space hydrogen-ring calculations reach 10,000 orbitals, with cyclic reduction providing further computational savings. These results show how exact reformulation, data structure exploitation and reuse of Coulomb actions make optimization of the selected large-scale SOS relaxation practical.

Yuming Bao, ..., Dongdong Ge, Yinyu Ye

item.title: [2★] Error Resilience and Unitary 2-Designs
item.author: Zheng-Hang Sun, ..., Xhek Turkeshi, Piotr Sierant
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 2 ★

Authors: Zheng-Hang Sun, ..., Xhek Turkeshi, Piotr Sierant

arXiv ID: 2611.14314 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Encoding-error-decoding circuits provide a setting for studying protection of quantum information against errors. In these circuits, an encoding unitary is followed by an error layer, decoding by the inverse unitary, and ancilla postselection. For encoders drawn from unitary 2-design ensembles, these circuits exhibit an error-protecting phase below a threshold error strength in which the fidelity between the input and recovered logical states approaches unity. Here, we show how departures from Haar second-moment statistics of the encoder can destabilize the error-protecting phase and derive a universal inequality linking recovery fidelity to the second unitary frame potential, which quantifies the ensemble's proximity to a unitary 2-design. This connection is exemplified by matchgate circuits doped with a tunable number of non-Gaussian gates. We analytically show that undoped circuits lack a stable error-protecting phase in the thermodynamic limit and that increasing the doping restores the error protection mechanism as the encoder ensemble approaches an approximate unitary 2-design. Further examples of Hamiltonian encoders, including an experimentally motivated all-to-all spin model, follow the same mechanism. Our results identify recovery fidelity as a diagnostic of departures from unitary 2-design behavior in quantum many-body systems.

Zheng-Hang Sun, ..., Xhek Turkeshi, Piotr Sierant

item.title: [2★] Quantum-Informed Graph Decomposition
item.author: Matthew Brunet, Leah Prepchuk, Rebekah Herrman
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 2 ★

Authors: Matthew Brunet, Leah Prepchuk, Rebekah Herrman

arXiv ID: 2611.14180 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) is a near-term quantum algorithm for solving combinatorial optimization problems, but its accuracy and resource requirements may scale poorly with problem size or structure, reducing its utility in practice. Approaches such as the Graph Decomposition for Optimization Algorithm (GDOA) seek to address this by iteratively reducing an input problem until it reaches a size where it can be solved using QAOA while maintaining the same optimal solution. This algorithm, however, requires solving integer programs that have exponentially many variables, and can result in suboptimal solutions, as the integer programs may contain slack terms. In this work, we propose a heuristic called the Quantum Enhanced Graph Decomposition (QEGD) algorithm. Its novelty lies in its use of QAOA as a subroutine for sparsifying a graph through local vertex-merging. The algorithm, when used to sparsify MaxCut problems that are then solved using QAOA, achieves higher approximation ratios across all tested graphs than GDOA for random 5-regular and 6-regular graphs. We then compare the time-to-solution and approximation ratio of QEGD to other QAOA variants a collection of Erdös-Rényi graphs. QEGD has higher approximation ratios on average than QAOA22^2 and ParaQAOA on all tested graphs. It also results in higher average approximation ratios than DC-QAOA on sparse Erdös-Rényi graphs and comparable average approximation ratio on denser Erdös-Rényi graphs. However, its average wall-clock time is between 0.4\% and 5\% of the average DC-QAOA wall-clock time.

Matthew Brunet, Leah Prepchuk, Rebekah Herrman

item.title: [2★] Multiparameter quantum estimation of circulant networks
item.author: Maria Popovic, ..., Ilaria Gianani, Claudia Benedetti
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 2 ★

Authors: Maria Popovic, ..., Ilaria Gianani, Claudia Benedetti

arXiv ID: 2611.13948 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Networks provide a natural description of interaction patterns, transport media, and communication architectures. Accurately characterizing their coupling structure is a key challenge in quantum technologies. We investigate the multiparameter quantum estimation of coupling strengths in circulant networks probed by continuous-time quantum walks. We derive the quantum Fisher information matrix, identify the optimal probe states and determine the ultimate precision allowed by quantum measurements, together with its scaling with the number of unknown couplings. We further analyze the precision achievable through position measurements of the walker, comparing the corresponding classical Cramér-Rao bounds for optimal and localized probe states with the quantum limit. Finally, we consider finite-resolution detection modeled by coarse-grained position measurements. Although coarse graining generally reduces estimation precision, we find that lower-resolution measurements can, in some instances, outperform other measurements with finer spatial resolution. Our results provide a systematic characterization of the fundamental and practical limits of coupling estimation in quantum-walk-based network inference.

Maria Popovic, ..., Ilaria Gianani, Claudia Benedetti

item.title: [2★] Parametric Proof-Carrying Compilation for Quantum Error-Correction
item.author: John Zhuoyang Ye, Jens Palsberg
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 2 ★

Authors: John Zhuoyang Ye, Jens Palsberg

arXiv ID: 2611.12985 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

We present PC-QEC, a proof-carrying compilation framework for quantum error correction parameterized by both code distance and syndrome-extraction scheme. It covers all four schemes---Standard, Flag, Shor and Knill---with circuit-level distance guarantees for every legal code distance in each proved family under the declared fault and readout contracts. The circuit-level model permits single-wire Pauli faults at every operation's qubit operands, capturing data errors, readout errors and ancilla faults that propagate into multi-qubit hook errors. For each family and scheme, code-algebra proofs and fault-aware Hoare proofs compose into a finite symbolic certificate whose size is independent of code distance. We demonstrate family-wide guarantees for five code families across all four schemes. For rotated Surface code, one Standard Scheme certificate proves a distance lower bound ddd for every odd d≥3d≥3d\ge3 and checks in 214\u2009s on average. Lean 4 mechanizes the metatheory and exact circuit-level distances for canonical Surface, hypergraph-product (HGP) and Toric code families.

John Zhuoyang Ye, Jens Palsberg

item.title: [1★] High-Speed Control of a Fluxonium Qubit via Picosecond Pulses from Josephson Digital Circuits
item.author: M. V. Bastrakova, ..., N. V. Klenov, I. I. Soloviev
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 1 ★

Authors: M. V. Bastrakova, ..., N. V. Klenov, I. I. Soloviev

arXiv ID: 2611.14358 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

We develop a control strategy for fluxonium qubits based on picosecond single-flux-quantum (SFQ) pulses generated by Josephson digital circuits. A major challenge is that SFQ protocols originally designed for transmon control become inefficient for low-frequency fluxonium. In this regime, the asymmetry of flux and charge couplings leads either to excessive leakage or excessively long gate times. We show that this limitation can be overcome by two complementary protocols. The first protocol employs high-frequency SFQ pulse packets applied through the flux channel, offering a simple, analytically transparent, and robust approach for high-fidelity single-qubit control. The second protocol combines phase-shifted flux and charge pulse sequences to enhance the resonant drive and reduce the gate duration. Multilevel simulations demonstrate single-qubit gate fidelities above 99.99%99.99%99.99\%; the simpler protocol remains robust under moderate variations of qubit parameters and flux bias, while the combined protocol preserves high fidelity while substantially accelerating the gate. These results establish SFQ-based cryogenic control as a realistic route to fast, accurate, and scalable manipulation of fluxonium qubits.

M. V. Bastrakova, ..., N. V. Klenov, I. I. Soloviev

item.title: [1★] Adaptive Policy-Guided Error Mitigation (APGEM): A Unified Learning-Based Framework for Noise Resilience in Quantum Machine Learning
item.author: Bisma Majid, Shabir Ahmad Sofi, Mir Mohammad Yousuf
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 1 ★

Authors: Bisma Majid, Shabir Ahmad Sofi, Mir Mohammad Yousuf

arXiv ID: 2611.13815 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Error mitigation stands between variational quantum algorithms and useful results on today's noisy hardware, yet in practice a mitigation method is usually chosen once, by hand, and applied unchanged for the life of an experiment. This is a poor fit for quantum machine learning (QML), where the circuit and the noise drift as training proceeds, so the best strategy in one regime is often wrong in another. We present a generalized form of Adaptive Policy-Guided Error Mitigation (APGEM), which treats the choice of mitigation technique as an online decision made from an algorithm's own feedback. A single contextual-bandit controller observes signals any variational algorithm already produces, such as fidelity, entropy, reward or loss, and gradient behavior, and selects among Zero-Noise Extrapolation, Probabilistic Error Cancellation, Measurement Error Mitigation, Dynamical Decoupling, and circuit optimization per step. Because it depends only on this shared feedback interface, the framework applies unchanged across supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement, and hybrid quantum-classical learning. Evaluated on five paradigms across 80 algorithm-and-noise conditions, adaptive selection reaches 95.5% of an oracle that always picks the best technique and significantly outperforms all six fixed strategies (Friedman χ2=92.18χ2=92.18\chi^{2}=92.18, p≈1.1×10−17p≈1.1×10−17p\approx1.1\times10^{-17}; pairwise Wilcoxon p<4×10−6p<4×10−6p<4\times10^{-6}). The learned policy is noise-aware: its favored technique shifts as depolarizing and readout error rise. On noise models from eight real IBM devices, APGEM tracks the oracle almost exactly (99.9% of oracle utility) at a flat cost of roughly 1.3×1041.3×1041.3\times10^{4} shots from three to eight qubits.

Bisma Majid, Shabir Ahmad Sofi, Mir Mohammad Yousuf

item.title: [1★] Coherent Optical Readout of Neutral-Atom Qubits via Homodyne Detection of Resonant Fluorescence
item.author: Minho Jang, ..., Sanghyo Park, Donggyu Kim
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 1 ★

Authors: Minho Jang, ..., Sanghyo Park, Donggyu Kim

arXiv ID: 2611.13799 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Fast, non-destructive qubit readout is essential for repeated sampling, mid-circuit measurement, and fault-tolerant neutral-atom quantum processing, but camera-based fluorescence detection introduces electronic latency beyond fluorescence-collection time. We propose coherent readout of the state-dependent resonant fluorescence using balanced homodyne detection with photodiodes. An analytic model quantifies the effect of atomic motion on the time-integrated quadrature signal and noise, showing that harmonic motion causes phase averaging while photon recoils produce trajectory-dependent signal fluctuations; the competition between signal accumulation and motion-induced decoherence sets an optimal detection time. Three-dimensional Monte Carlo simulations validate the model and predict state-detection fidelities exceeding 99% within 100 μsμs\mu\mathrm{s} for experimentally realistic parameters. These results establish the readout conditions and physical constraints for rapid coherent fluorescence readout of neutral-atom qubits.

Minho Jang, ..., Sanghyo Park, Donggyu Kim

item.title: [1★] A Hardware-Trained Generative Quantum Eigensolver for Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization of Organotin Hydroxides up to 70 Qubits
item.author: Kunal Kumar, ..., Toru Imai, Takayuki Osogami
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 1 ★

Authors: Kunal Kumar, ..., Toru Imai, Takayuki Osogami

arXiv ID: 2611.13755 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Quantum hardware can provide feedback for training circuit generators beyond the reach of exact classical simulation. We train generative quantum eigensolver (GQE) policies, transformers conditioned on molecular descriptors, to generate the state-preparation circuits for sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD). Training runs first on a noiseless simulator and then with the IBM Heron processor ibm_kobe inside the loop, at 46 and 70 qubits (1.2×1081.2×1081.2 \times 10^8 shots for the four main training runs). A classical CCSD(T) reference energy of the training molecules enters only an admission gate and two auxiliary reward terms. During hardware training, a reward penalty prevents collapse to circuits that sample only the Hartree-Fock determinant. Policies trained on transition-metal complexes are applied without retraining to Sn(OH)33_3-Me and its hydrates, minimal models of organotin photoresists for extreme-ultraviolet lithography, from 32 to 70 qubits. After one round of hardware sampling, followed by classical ranking and recovery of the cached counts with the molecular Hamiltonian and no further QPU calls, 27 of 28 runs at 46-70 qubits are within 15 mHa of the density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) reference (median 4.5 mHa), and in all eight runs with an untrained control the trained policy is more accurate. At 56-70 qubits the selected circuits use 34-72 times fewer two-qubit gates than the local unitary cluster Jastrow (LUCJ) circuit transpiled for the same device. These results demonstrate that circuit generators can be trained with quantum hardware at 70 qubits.

Kunal Kumar, ..., Toru Imai, Takayuki Osogami

item.title: [1★] Computational Power of Clifford and Ising Quantum Computers
item.author: Sawyer Dobson, Zhenghan Wang
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 1 ★

Authors: Sawyer Dobson, Zhenghan Wang

arXiv ID: 2611.13347 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

We extend the efficient classical simulation of Ising quantum computers from braidings to measurements. We investigate several different definitions of efficient Clifford quantum computation by varying the power of the circuit generator. In case the circuit generator can see the entire input, we give a detailed proof that efficient simulation of classical computation would imply the separation of complexity classes P\mathbf{P} and PSPACE\mathbf{PSPACE}. If the circuit generator sees only the input length, we prove that Clifford quantum computers decide what we call affine languages.

item.title: [1★] Quantized memory of measurement records near the light cone of quantum circuits
item.author: Jamal Slim
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 1 ★

Authors: Jamal Slim

arXiv ID: 2611.13175 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Quantum processors now measure qubits in the middle of a circuit, and the stream of outcomes is the raw output of error correction, measurement-based state preparation and monitored dynamics. For a scrambling circuit, predicting the statistics of this stream is as hard as simulating the processor, so there is no exact reference to check it against once the device outgrows classical simulation. We show that near the light cone the problem becomes exactly solvable, for any two-qubit gate. In a brickwork circuit with one polarized qubit in a maximally mixed background, measurements along the edge of the light cone form a two-state Markov chain, and measurements dd sites inside the edge are generated by ⌊d/2⌋+1\lfloor d/2\rfloor+1 qubits that move with it, while the rest of the chain, however large, acts on them as a memoryless bath. The memory of the record is therefore quantized, one bit on the edge and at most one more for every site of displacement, a bound that generic gates attain. The same causal structure determines which hardware noise the record can see, removes that sensitivity at no gate cost, and yields a tomography-free witness of dual-unitarity. On a 156-qubit superconducting processor, a demonstration with its analysis specified in advance finds the predicted memory one and two sites inside the light cone, and none where the theory forbids it. This gives dynamic circuits an exact reference at any system size, and shows that the collision models of open-system theory arise exactly inside chaotic dynamics.

Jamal Slim

item.title: [1★] Long-range correlated quantum errors from diffuson-correlated dephasing
item.author: N. R. S. van Venrooij, M. E. Flatté
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 1 ★

Authors: N. R. S. van Venrooij, M. E. Flatté

arXiv ID: 2611.13156 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Electrical solid-state qubits are generally initialized, manipulated and read out through diffusive conductors. We show that the disorder-induced low energy modes of such a conductor --- diffusons --- impose spatially correlated dephasing on any qubits that share it, a mechanism we term diffuson-correlated dephasing. Starting from a Keldysh nonlinear sigma model for the disordered conductive region, coupled capacitively to two-level systems, we obtain the noise kernel in closed form. It decays as the inverse square of the qubit separation and changes sign with the orientation of the pair, so that qubit pairs at equal separation may be correlated or anticorrelated, an unambiguous experimental signature. In two dimensions, the correlated noise a single qubit shares with the rest of the array, in the worst-case scenario, grows logarithmically with array size rather than converging. The sufficient condition for fault tolerance under correlated noise is therefore violated, so standard threshold theorems no longer guarantee protection against this channel for large qubit arrays. As this dephasing originates from the soft-mode content of the environment rather than on any specific gate detail, we expect correlated dephasing channels of this kind wherever solid-state qubits or sensors share a gapless conductive medium.

N. R. S. van Venrooij, M. E. Flatté

item.title: [1★] Dynamics of Rényi entanglement entropies and Eigenstate Thermalization
item.author: Riccardo Senese, Pasquale Calabrese
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 1 ★

Authors: Riccardo Senese, Pasquale Calabrese

arXiv ID: 2611.13141 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

How is entanglement dynamics encoded in the eigenstates of the time-evolution operator? We address this question by focusing on Rényi entropy dynamics in deterministic chaotic Floquet models in arbitrary dimensions. Inspired by the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH), we employ spectral representations of reduced density matrix moments (purity and its higher-order generalizations) whose decay through spectral dephasing captures nonequilibrium entanglement growth. These representations closely resemble those governing local-observable dynamics, but involve eigenstates in a replicated Hilbert space and observables are replaced by subsystem permutation operators, such as the swap operator for Rényi-2. Focusing on Rényi-2, we combine exact random matrix theory calculations, established ETH results and numerical tests in 1D to formulate ETH-like ansätze for subsystem swap matrix elements in the replicated eigenbasis and their cross-correlations with initial-state overlap statistics. In the thermodynamic limit, purity dynamics is entirely determined by smooth slowly varying functions that emerge from such statistics, paralleling generalized ETH formulations in a single replica. In the limit of large subsystems, these functions exhibit a striking structural simplification: locality of the dynamics together with bulk spectral dephasing reduce their functional dependence to a single fundamental frequency. Our formalism provides a setting where ETH-like statements naturally coexist for both arbitrarily small and large subsystem sizes. We discuss extensions of our results to higher Rényi entropies. Beyond clarifying the spectral foundations of entanglement dynamics, these results lay some of the groundwork for future applications of spectral filter methods to the computation of Rényi evolution in deterministic systems.

Riccardo Senese, Pasquale Calabrese

item.title: [1★] Time Direction Entanglement Entropy of Free Fermion Ground States
item.author: Xinyu Sun, ..., Joshua Yi, Biao Lian
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 1 ★

Authors: Xinyu Sun, ..., Joshua Yi, Biao Lian

arXiv ID: 2611.13085 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

While the entanglement entropy of a spatial subregion has been extensively studied, a properly defined entanglement entropy of quantum states in a time direction interval remains underexplored. We investigate the scaling behaviors of the recently defined time direction entanglement entropy (TDEE) for free fermion quantum states, which is computed from the reduced density matrix of a sub-Hilbert space that minimally supports all the time-evolved operators in the time direction interval. Based on the Fisher--Hartwig conjecture for Toeplitz matrices, we develop an analytical framework for understanding the TDEE in a time interval with discrete time step τ\tau. For disorderless one-dimensional (1D) systems (gapless fermions or band insulators), in different regimes of gap, bandwidth and τ\tau, we find the TDEE can exhibit area law (for nonzero gap), logarithmic law or volume law in the length of time. For 1D Anderson insulators, we numerically find the TDEE shows a Page-curve like behavior, growing at short time, and decaying in power-law at long time exceeding the crossover time determined by localization. In the continuum time limit τ→0\tau\rightarrow 0, the TDEE of disorderless gapless fermions, band insulators and Anderson insulators exhibit logarithmic law, area law and sub-area law, respectively. We also show that the sub-Hilbert space of a time-direction interval stabilizes in the τ→0\tau\rightarrow 0 limit, which is understandable as a subspace of the Hilbert space of the Lieb-Robinson causal diamond.

Xinyu Sun, ..., Joshua Yi, Biao Lian

item.title: [1★] Tripartite nonlocal magic from reflected and negativity spectra
item.author: Sriram Akella
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 1 ★

Authors: Sriram Akella

arXiv ID: 2611.13071 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

A tripartite pure state is local-unitary equivalent to a stabilizer state if and only if its marginal, reflected, and negativity spectra (up to signs) are flat. These conditions are quantified using anti-flatness, giving a diagnostic of tripartite nonlocal magic that is computable and experimentally measurable using randomized measurements. In non-abelian quantum doubles, it appears only when the triple points of the tripartition lie on plaquettes. In random tensor networks, it appears exactly when the entanglement wedge of two boundary regions connects.

item.title: [1★] Time Running Backwards, and Where It Stops: Superoscillations of Proper Time and the Memory of the Environment
item.author: Yakir Aharonov, Avshalom C. Elitzur

Authors: Yakir Aharonov, Avshalom C. Elitzur

arXiv ID: 2611.12971 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

A quantum system prepared in a superposition of proper times - a clock whose worldline is superposed, or a clock at rest in a superposed gravitational potential - evolves, in each branch, by the same dynamics for a different duration. Post-selecting the control that sets the proper time turns the superposition into a superoscillation of the time-dilation factor: the system is found to have evolved for a proper time αwt\alpha_w t, where the weak value αw\alpha_w may exceed unity, vanish, or be negative - the quantum time-translation machine of Aharonov, Anandan, Popescu and Vaidman. We ask how far back such a machine can run an irreversible process. The test system is a sealed cell - excited atoms, the radiation field they emit into, and the absorbing walls, carried as one quantum object - and the witness is projective: atoms that had begun to decay before the run are found, in the post-selected sub-ensemble, more excited than when inserted. The answer is exact and depends only on the atoms' survival amplitude. With two branches the witness holds only while the decay is younger than the memory time of the environment, after which the emission becomes Markovian. Beyond it, the post-selection amplifies the minute difference between the contents of the cell in the two branches, set by the full energy spread of the atoms and their field rather than by the linewidth, and the witness fails. Reversing a decay past the memory time requires many branches, an environment with a strictly bounded spectrum, and a post-selection probability that falls exponentially with the number of environmental oscillations to be undone. The obstacle to reversal is therefore not entropy but bandwidth - the same bandwidth that makes the emission irreversible in the first place. We give four ways to superpose a clock rate, from ...

item.title: [0★] Finite-Key Readiness and Authentication-Key Replenishment in QKD-Assisted UAV Edge Computing
item.author: Dang H. Le, Ban Q. Tran, Susan Mengel
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 0 ★

Authors: Dang H. Le, Ban Q. Tran, Susan Mengel

arXiv ID: 2611.14461 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

A service that needs fresh quantum keys must wait for key release, and may be denied it, before protected computation starts. We quantify this cost for a trusted stationary UAV serving two ground gateways, each obtaining its keys from one finite-key decoy-state BB84 attempt with parameters fixed in advance. A count-level Monte Carlo model, reproduced by a semi-analytic model, links key acceptance to protected upload, computation, and download, including failed attempts and hover energy. At 26~dB effective optical loss, with authentication hashing at its proxy-benchmarked, near-zero cost, fresh keys raise the 95th-percentile completion time of both tasks from 10.37 to 28.65~s; hover energy grows in proportion. The scalar rate models evaluated here miss the deadline limit on the block size. The pulse budget lies in a window bounded below by authentication-key replenishment and above by the deadline; for a fixed source, channel, and acceptance model, the authentication debit shifts the floor, whereas hashing cost does not. At a 35-s deadline the largest tested loss with a non-empty window is 27~dB at 1\% misalignment and 22~dB at 2\%; at 3\% no tested setting has one. Conditional on the assumed acquisition probability, the selected configurations meet this deadline with simultaneous lower confidence bounds of 96.9--97.3\% on held-out trials, at 26~dB and at 18--20~dB with 2\% misalignment. A high-cost stress reference that charges hashing in full narrows the window and lowers these loss limits to 26 and 20~dB at the reference processing capacity. A small rise in error rate or loss pushes the deadline probability well below its target and drains authentication keys, while the protocol's security parameter is unchanged.

Dang H. Le, Ban Q. Tran, Susan Mengel

item.title: [0★] Structure of correlations for the single-jj model using quantum information theory
item.author: Javier Faba, Vicente Martín, Luis Robledo
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 0 ★

Authors: Javier Faba, Vicente Martín, Luis Robledo

arXiv ID: 2611.14460 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

We say that a system undergoes a quantum phase transition when the mean-field ground state of a given Hamiltonian spontaneously breaks its symmetries depending on the Hamiltonian parameters. It is a widely accepted view that this phenomenon enables the mean-field state to absorb the maximum amount of correlations without losing its mean-field structure. However, it is still uncertain how those correlations are incorporated within the mean-field state and how the correlation structure changes when we get closer to the exact ground state by restoring the symmetries. In this work, we answer these questions by studying the single-jj model, which is a realistic fermionic nuclear model with abelian and non-abelian broken symmetries. We find that both types of symmetries have very different effects for the correlations within the mean-field state. This makes unclear the concept of the symmetry breaking process as a mechanism to absorb the maximum amount of correlations. Moreover, the symmetry restoration redistributes existing `fake' correlations between paired orbitals to more complex subsystems.

Javier Faba, Vicente Martín, Luis Robledo

item.title: [0★] Quantum Thermal Transistor via Nonlinear Environmental Coupling
item.author: Laiba Hayat, M. Tahir Naseem
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 0 ★

Authors: Laiba Hayat, M. Tahir Naseem

arXiv ID: 2611.14458 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Thermal amplification enables sensitive control of heat currents, providing a basis for heat management and thermal signal processing in quantum devices. For a harmonic oscillator coupled to emitter, collector, and base thermal reservoirs, we recover the absence of thermal amplification when system-reservoir interactions permit only single-quantum exchange. A controlled weak-nonlinearity expansion, supported by numerical stationary solutions, shows that two-quantum exchange at the emitter enables amplification and predicts its onset. When two-quantum exchange dominates at the emitter and collector, varying the base temperature redistributes populations between even and odd oscillator sectors. This changes the emitter and collector heat currents far more than the base current, enabling large thermal amplification. We propose a realization using a longitudinally coupled auxiliary two-level system and bath spectral filtering, specifying conditions for its elimination to yield the required oscillator dynamics. These results establish nonlinear system-reservoir coupling as a resource for controlling heat flow and enabling thermal amplification.

Laiba Hayat, M. Tahir Naseem

item.title: [0★] Operational limits of reference renewal for retained quantum-service results
item.author: Roberto Fernández-Barrios, ..., Amaia Pikatza-Huerga, Pablo García Bringas
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 0 ★

Authors: Roberto Fernández-Barrios, ..., Amaia Pikatza-Huerga, Pablo García Bringas

arXiv ID: 2611.14376 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

item.content:encoded:
Scites: 0 ★

Authors: Dorota M. Grabowska

arXiv ID: 2611.13886 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

We present a lattice Hamiltonian for chiral gauge theories on the boundary of a slab. The formulation is gauge-fixed, so the gauge variables are the physical modes of the boundary field, and Gauss's law holds exactly. The bulk gauge field is determined by the boundary field and an integer label, which is the topological charge that the boundary generates and the bulk stores as a localized instanton. The bulk enters as a dielectric, and both gauge anomaly conditions become the question of whether the boundary satisfies Gauss's law on its own. For background gauge fields, we show that sectors that differ by a unit of bulk charge are degenerate after Pauli-Villars subtraction and the mirror fermions decouple. The boundary theory has no vacuum angle. Every term in the Hamiltonian is defined in terms of the boundary gauge variables, the integer label and the fermion modes, a starting point for quantum circuit construction.

item.title: [0★] Assessing the expressive power of a gauge-invariant PEPS ansatz across a topological phase transition
item.author: Etsuko Itou, Tsuyoshi Okubo
item.content:encoded:

Authors: Etsuko Itou, Tsuyoshi Okubo

arXiv ID: 2611.13852 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

We investigate the expressive power of the gauged Gaussian fermionic projected entangled pair state (GGFPEPS) ansatz, which is a manifestly gauge-invariant tensor network ansatz for (2+1)(2+1)(2+1)-dimensional lattice gauge theories. In the GGFPEPS ansatz, the gauge field on each link is represented by coupling its configuration to the fermion number of virtual fermions placed at both ends of the link. This ansatz has been studied by variational Monte Carlo (VMC) methods in previous work~\citeEmonts:2022yom. However, the statistical error of VMC makes a precise determination of the variational parameters difficult, so that the expressive power of the ansatz could not be examined accurately. In this work, we reformulate the computation as a Grassmann tensor network (TN), in which the whole network is contracted deterministically, and introduce the higher-order tensor renormalization group (HOTRG), which allows us to perform calculations in large volumes up to L=34L=34L=34. We also evaluate the infinite volume system using the corner transfer matrix renormalization group (CTMRG). We find that the ansatz with only eight complex variational parameters accurately describes the pure Z2\mathbb{Z}_2 gauge theory including the region of the topological phase transition, not only in the energy but also in the topological entanglement entropy. The critical coupling obtained from the peaks of their susceptibilities agrees quantitatively with the one predicted by continuous-time quantum Monte Carlo simulations~\citewu2012phase. Furthermore, near the transition point, we show that the ansatz represents a state outside the plaquette product family, which is a one-parameter family of states assumed in the construction of the ansatz as a simple interpolation between the strong and weak coupling limits.

Etsuko Itou, Tsuyoshi Okubo

arXiv ID: 2611.13796 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

We theoretically investigate an analog implementation of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) for the weighted maximum cut problem (MaxCut) problem. The protocol uses a three-dimensional array of individually trapped Rydberg atoms driven by globally addressed laser pulses, with site-dependent detunings applied near the Rydberg resonance. As benchmarks, we consider twenty randomly weighted 3-regular graphs with 12 vertices each. Problem weights are encoded directly in the interatomic interaction energies by choosing appropriate three-dimensional atom positions. We compare two parameter-optimization strategies: discretized quantum annealing and warm-start initialization using a graph neural network (GNN). The combined optimization strategy creates a portfolio that outperforms the Goemans-Williamson (GW) rounding almost in all instances in the noiseless case. We analyze the sampling statistics and the total pulse-time cost of both approaches. Finally, we emulate the performance of the optimized schedules on quantum trajectories using a realistic error model of the Aquila neutral-atom quantum processor.

Abstract:

Superconducting resonator arrays can tailor the photonic environment for quantum information processing, but conventional port-based microwave spectroscopy alone does not resolve the rich spatial structure of their modes. Our work establishes a combined spatial characterization approach for compact superconducting resonator arrays with applications in hybrid spin--superconducting quantum systems.

Abstract:

Generative approaches to this problem can make use of a "latent" or "prior" data representation, which is often chosen to be a Gaussian distribution. Authors: Yu-Kun Lu, Jiahao Lyu, Wolfgang Ketterle

arXiv ID: 2611.13665 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

We have prepared pairs of atoms at densities exceeding 1016/cm3 10^{16}/\rm{cm}^3 corresponding to n\lambdabar3>10n\lambdabar^3>10 and studied how they interact with light. In this regime, the coherent part of the electric dipole-dipole interaction is larger than the dissipative part, and a single photon emission can transfer large momenta (larger than ten times the single photon recoil) to the atoms. For two atoms, the resonance is shifted by the two-body Lamb shift which is dominated by the near-field part of the dipolar interaction. Dipolar resonance shifts have been observed before only for many atoms interacting with the far-field part of the dipolar interaction. Our work sheds new light on photoassociation processes and paves the way for studying driven quantum systems with strong electric dipole-dipole interactions.

Authors: Tae Yeong Park, ..., Paul G. Kwiat, Hee Su Park

arXiv ID: 2611.13625 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

The ability to dynamically route quantum information across multiple nodes is a key requirement for realizing versatile and scalable quantum networks. Quantum routers are devices to achieve packet-level routing beyond static point-to-point connections by handling hybrid packets combining classical headers and quantum payloads. Previously proposed methods have selectively accessed the classical and quantum components of the packets utilizing wavelength splitters and optical switches, and repacked the hybrid packets before transmission through the outgoing link with regenerating classical headers. This work reports a novel optical-fiber-based quantum router that minimizes the disturbance and latency on the hybrid packets through more transparent operation. We experimentally demonstrate double-hop routing via two cascaded routers to three distinct receivers without regeneration of the headers. As a practical application, quantum key distribution packets based on time-bin qubits and a BB84 protocol with a two-decoy-state method are successfully delivered to the three receivers achieving nonzero secret key rates. These results demonstrate the feasibility of extensive quantum networks interconnected by multiple-step router nodes.

Authors: Lizhong Fu, Honghui Shang, Jinlong Yang

arXiv ID: 2611.13522 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Second-order Epstein-Nesbet perturbation theory (EN-PT2) is an important tool for improving selected configuration interaction (SCI) energies, but the large external determinant space creates substantial memory and communication costs on GPU clusters. We develop a fully GPU-accelerated implementation of distributed semistochastic EN-PT2, fusing excitation generation, screening, and PT2 weighting in a single kernel traversal. Applications to an iron-oxo complex in a (60e, 187o) active space, iron-porphyrin references containing 200 million determinants per state, and neural-network quantum states establish the method's efficiency for perturbative corrections to large reference wave functions in the GPU era.

item.title: [0★] Quantum-walk transport oracles and amplitude estimation of a scalar range statistic in proton therapy
item.author: Kwangzoo Chung
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 0 ★

Authors: Kwangzoo Chung

arXiv ID: 2611.13475 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Quantum amplitude estimation (QAE) promises a quadratic reduction in the sampling cost of Monte Carlo (MC) particle transport, but two obstacles have kept it from radiotherapy physics: the lack of an efficient unitary encoding of charged-particle transport, and the mismatch between QAE's single-scalar output and the per-voxel structure of dose calculation. We address both. We construct a discrete-time quantum-walk transport oracle for protons in which an energy register is driven by an energy-dependent coin encoding a continuous-slowing-down surrogate of the stopping power, so that stochastic energy loss and range straggling follow from the circuit dynamics. The oracle is unitary, with one fresh coin qubit per step, and its gate count grows linearly in the number of energy levels. On it we formulate a scalar range statistic, the probability that a proton penetrates beyond a distal depth threshold, as a directly marked amplitude, and estimate it by maximum-likelihood amplitude estimation (MLQAE) with Grover iterations and finite shots. The oracle reproduces a Bragg-shaped depth-deposit profile agreeing with a classical MC of identical rules to within 0.27%, and Grover amplification matches sin2((2k+1)θ)\sin^2((2k+1)\theta) to machine precision up to k=32k=32. At matched budget the MLQAE error falls as N−0.93N^{-0.93} against N−0.49N^{-0.49} for sampling, 4.8 times smaller at the largest budget. A three-gate resource analysis (output structure, amortization, error-corrected wall-clock) finds full dose maps structurally unfavourable irrespective of hardware, and the scalar statistic short of a wall-clock crossover at clinical scale: the oracle's derived cost of 1.0×1061.0 \times 10^6 logical gates per call (3.5×1073.5 \times 10^7 with rotation synthesis), dominated by the multiplexed coin, is 160 to 5400 times the permitted budget. We report the reduction that would be required and identify the term responsible for it.

Authors: Diego Aranda-Lozano, ..., Ricardo Román-Ancheyta, Carlos A. González-Gutiérrez

Abstract:

We study the time-dependent physical spectrum of light for a two-level atom coupled to a large, but discrete, number of modes of an electromagnetic cavity. Radiation emitted by the atom, placed at the center of the cavity, returns after the round-trip time trt_r, re-excites it, and is re-emitted, producing a sequence of atomic population revivals. For a coupling approximately flat over the atomic linewidth, the emission dynamics reduces to a delay-differential equation of Bixon--Jortner type. Using its analytical solution in terms of Laguerre polynomials, we investigate how successive emission and reabsorption cycles shape the time-dependent spectrum. The physical spectrum exhibits revivals during which a transient frequency comb of spacing 2π/tr2\pi/t_r develops. The comb results from the quantum interference between successive emission stages; its teeth sit not at the cavity modes but at the resonances of the effective two half-cavities created by the resonantly reflecting atom. The visibility scales as e−Γtre^{-\Gamma t_r} with the filter bandwidth Γ\Gamma, and at long times the comb converges to the dressed-mode spectrum, which we also obtain analytically in quantitative agreement with exact diagonalization. We show that the physical spectrum resolves the feedback phase, to which the atomic population is insensitive in the regime of well-separated emission stages, and provides additional frequency-resolved signatures of the atomic position. We discuss two feasible experimental implementations of our results with transmons (artificial atoms) coupled to microwave and surface-acoustic-wave resonators.

Abstract:

The negatively charged boron vacancy (V−BV_{\mathrm{B}}^{-}) in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) is a promising spin defect for quantum sensing in two-dimensional material systems. Previous hBN experiments have mainly exploited the two spin-triplet ground-state single-quantum transitions separately. Here we implement a double-quantum driving scheme based on simultaneous resonant microwave excitation of both ground-state single-quantum transitions, establishing coherent control of the Δms=2\Delta m_s=2 manifold in a V−BV_{\mathrm{B}}^{-} ensemble. We compare the resulting double-quantum response with the corresponding single-quantum protocol under identical experimental conditions. The double-quantum protocol enhances the optical readout contrast and yields a 2.6-fold signal-to-noise improvement in AC magnetometry. We further use the double-quantum relaxation channel as a differential probe of electric-field and strain noise, showing that the present data are compatible with correlated-surface or volume-distributed fluctuations, while short-range uncorrelated surface-noise models are disfavored within the assumptions of our analysis. These results establish double-quantum coherent control and frequency-resolved AC magnetometry in hBN spin ensembles, and identify the sample-dependent measurements needed to determine the microscopic origin of the dominant relaxation channels.

arXiv ID: 2611.13221 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

An exceptional point of a memory-coefficient equation need not have the same signature in every quantum-state observable. We examine this relation within exact non-Markovian quantum-state diffusion (NMQSD), following the same operator closure from its coefficient dynamics to the non-Markovian master equation obtained by noise averaging. A finite homogeneous lift identifies the Jordan chains reached by the causal initialization, while state reconstruction determines which contributions survive in a specified readout. Two models expose the distinction. For common-bath qubits restricted to zero and one excitation, a noise-independent lowering-form OO operator gives a closed master equation. Every defective decaying mode transfers its full pole order to a suitable unconditional excitation--reference coherence. A known third-order configuration illustrates both a quadratic--exponential coherence and cancellation of its highest-order term in another quadrature. For a position-coupled oscillator in a fixed-photon-number optomechanical sector, the exact closure contains a scalar noise-history term. On the regular normalizable branch studied for bath decay rates below the oscillator frequency, two second-order coefficient blocks lead to a double pole in the conditional displacement response to the NMQSD noise history, at long preparation age and fixed lag. The purely algebraic coefficient tail cancels from the conditional Gaussian width. Complete noise averaging changes the master-equation coefficients and combines conditional width with the weighted spread of state centers. Together, the models show how causal preparation, state reconstruction, and averaging give coefficient exceptional points a precise, readout-dependent meaning.

Abstract:

We introduce a finite-memory repeat-until-success (RUS) framework for implementing rational spectral filters on a quantum computer, extending spectral filtering beyond the polynomial transformations implemented by quantum signal processing (QSP) and quantum singular value transformation (QSVT). Our approach interleaves queries to a block encoding of a Hermitian operator XX, whose spectrum lies in [−1,1][-1,1], and mid-circuit measurements that either accept, reject, or continue the computation without resetting the quantum state. Abstract:

Abstract:

item.author: Mahmoud Abdelshafy, Joaquin F. Rodriguez-Nieva
item.content:encoded:

Authors: Mahmoud Abdelshafy, Joaquin F. Rodriguez-Nieva

arXiv ID: 2611.13101 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Quantum-chaotic systems share the same coarse-grained features characteristic of random matrices, such as Wigner-Dyson level-spacing statistics, yet can exhibit strikingly different eigenstate structure and many-body dynamics, including relaxation, transport, scrambling, and entanglement growth. This raises the fundamental question of whether these finer-grained features probe genuinely distinct aspects of quantum chaos or, instead, reflect different manifestations of a common underlying structure---and whether such structure provides a meaningful basis for regarding one many-body quantum system as "more chaotic" than another. Here, we address this question by introducing a quantum geometric framework that quantifies the susceptibility of many-body eigenstates to physically allowed deformations of the Hamiltonian, as constrained by spatial locality, symmetries, and conservation laws. The resulting geometric susceptibility is quantitative, providing a metric of chaos beyond traditional binary diagnostics; intrinsic, as it depends on the manifold of allowed Hamiltonian deformations rather than on the way the system is probed; and unifying, as it directly connects eigenstate structure with dynamics. For canonical models of quantum chaos, we find that minimal geometric susceptibility, maximal eigenstate randomness, broad spectral response of local operators, and the suppression of nonhydrodynamic slow structure coalesce in the same region of Hamiltonian control space. This suggests that these seemingly distinct signatures of chaos are different manifestations of a common underlying geometric structure. Our framework provides a route toward understanding the limits of relaxation and scrambling under physical constraints; in applications, it offers a means to engineer strongly chaotic regimes in programmable quantum systems with restricted controls.

Mahmoud Abdelshafy, Joaquin F. Rodriguez-Nieva

Abstract:

Randomized measurements offer a way to probe nonlinear properties of quantum states without reconstructing their full density matrices. For states shared between distant laboratories, we study products of three outcome probabilities measured at the same local settings and then averaged over independent local random unitaries. We determine, for an arbitrary number of parties, which third-order local-unitary invariant combinations these averages retain and which they cannot separate. The accessible information is encoded in algebraic invariants of the quantum state and is reconstructed by analysing the permutation symmetries induced by the distributed measurement protocol. Exploiting these symmetries, the reconstruction problem collapses, regardless of the number of measurement outcomes, to the symbolic inversion of a 3 x 3 matrix. As a result, nonlinear information can be extracted without inverting the exponentially large matrices that typically arise in distributed multipartite quantum systems.

Abstract:

We apply the large NN matrix bootstrap technique to constrain expectation values of simple operators in heavy BPS states that are dual to classical geometries. For states dual to horizonless geometries, their explicit moduli give rise to large allowable regions in the bootstrap, while for black holes, a converging bootstrap should find islands. We explore this method in N=4\mathcal{N}=4 SU(N)SU(N) super Yang-Mills theory at large NN, working at weak coupling and focusing on BPS states with scaling dimensions of order N2N^2. For the 1/21/2, 1/41/4, and 1/81/8-BPS sectors, the bootstrap finds large regions, in agreement with an eigenvalue description of such states in the limit of large charges. We also present preliminary results for a BMN truncation of the 1/161/16-BPS sector, which contains states dual to both horizonless geometries and black holes. Abstract:

Superconducting Josephson traveling wave parametric amplifiers (JTWPAs) enable broadband, quantum-limited amplification of weak microwave signals. JTWPAs are essential for the single-shot readout of superconducting qubits, broadband vacuum squeezing, or the generation of microwave cluster states. Phase-matching between signal and pump modes in such JTWPAs represents a major engineering challenge, which is typically solved by integrating resonators in a nonlinear medium in order to tailor electromagnetic dispersion relations and achieve a broadband, high-gain amplification. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a phase-matching approach using a homogeneous nonlinear medium based on Josephson elements by exploiting a magnetic field inhomogeneity. We show how the latter may lead to the sign reversal of the 3-wave mixing nonlinearity and stabilization of the parametric amplification. We envision this technique as a viable alternative to conventional phase-matching approaches.
